To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the maximum capacity of a wireless ad hoc network may be approximated in polynomial time by solving an NP-complete problem, and that the resulting approximation is good for networks that arise in wireless ad hoc networking.

the maximum number of simultaneous concurrent transmissions in an ad hoc wireless network may be modeled as the problem of finding a maximum distance-2 edge matching in the underlying network, and that this problem can be approximated in polynomial time.

1) D2EMIS, which we define and show is NP-complete, is a natural and useful abstraction of a class of MAC protocols that include 802.11; 2) D2EMIs in disk graphs can be approximated well; 3) this approximation yields good bounds on the maximum network capacity for these graphs; 4) we present a distributed algorithm for D2EMIs on unit disk graphs; and 5) we outline extensions of our results.
In summary, our research is concerned with
determining a "maximum" measure for the capacity of wireless networks, and with approximating it efficiently.
the fundamental problem of estimating the maximum capacity of wireless networks.
the fundamental problem of computing an upper bound on the maximum network capacity in wireless networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the distance-2 matching model is a useful model for approximating the maximum MAC-layer capacity of ad hoc networks, and that our algorithm provides a simple, yet powerful, method for estimating the maximum MAC-layer capacities of ad hoc wireless network.
the MAC-layer capacity of ad hoc networks is NP-complete and that it can be efficiently approximated.
our work is the first to provide an approximation for the maximum capacity of wireless ad hoc networks, and to relate it to the problem of determining "good" topologies in such networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it shows how to compute a good approximation for a fundamental network capacity measure, for a large class wireless networks, and in a distributed fashion.

it provides the first efficient approximation algorithm for the maximum capacity of a wireless ad hoc network, and the first efficient approximation for a large class (including disk graphs) of wireless network models.
we show that D2EMIS, a natural graph-theoretic problem, captures the MAC capacity of ad hoc networks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the MAC layer is the first and foremost layer in wireless networks that needs to be addressed, it is not a trivial problem.
the maximum MAC capacity of a wireless network can be approximated very efficiently.
the maximum capacity of ad hoc networks is a function of the underlying graph structure, and can be approximated well using a distributed algorithm that is simple to implement.
